summary: Describes how to use TESLA, a scheme that lets receivers check that packets really came from the claimed sender and were not altered, in the ALC and NORM multicast content delivery protocols. It covers only authenticating the sender's packets, not those sent by receivers. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A teacher stamps every handout with a special seal, so students in a big hall can tell real handouts from fakes slipped in by someone else.

questions: how does tesla authenticate multicast packets
what is the tesla group mac
subtitle: How a multicast sender proves its packets are real by revealing signing keys a little later, in the ALC and NORM protocols.

tldr.problem: In multicast, every receiver needs to be sure a packet came from the real sender, but a shared group key lets any member forge packets and digital signatures on every packet are costly.
tldr.mechanism: TESLA has the sender MAC each packet with a key from a one-way key chain and reveal that key only d intervals later, so receivers hold packets until the key arrives and then verify them. Receivers need loosely synchronized clocks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5776 defines the bootstrap and authentication messages and an EXT_AUTH header extension for ALC and NORM. It is an Experimental document and covers only packets from the sender, not receiver feedback.

today: RFC 5776 is an Experimental document, published in April 2010. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Authenticating Multicast Senders
sections.content:
ALC and NORM are two content delivery protocols that move objects such as files from one sender to many receivers. ALC works over purely one-way channels and repeats data in a carousel or uses forward error correction. NORM has receivers send acknowledgments and ask for retransmissions.

The goal is to stop an attacker from impersonating the sender and injecting forged packets that corrupt the objects receivers rebuild. With one receiver, a shared secret and a MAC (message authentication code) would do. With a group, a shared key lets any member forge packets, and digital signatures on every packet cost too much computing and space.

TESLA (Timed Efficient Stream Loss-tolerant Authentication) is the alternative. This RFC explains how to integrate it into ALC and NORM, so applications on top, such as FLUTE, benefit automatically. Only the sender's packets are covered. Authenticating receivers' packets, such as NORM feedback, is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When many people listen to one speaker, a shared password would let any listener pretend to be the speaker. TESLA gives the speaker a way to prove who is talking without that problem.

sections.title: Intervals, Key Chains and Delayed Disclosure
sections.content:
The sender divides time into equal intervals of length T_int, numbered from 0. It builds a one-way key chain of N+1 keys, K_0 to K_N. It starts from a random primary key K_N and computes each earlier key as K_{i-1} = F(K_i), where F is a one-way function built from a pseudo-random function. Each interval gets one key, used in reverse order, and the MAC key is derived as K'_i = F'(K_i).

A packet sent in interval i carries a MAC made with K'_i, but not that key. The key K_i is disclosed only d intervals later, and d MUST be at least 2. Because anyone can run F forward from a later key to check an earlier one, a receiver can verify a disclosed key against any key it already trusts.

If a session outlasts one chain, the sender switches to a new chain of the same length. It sends a commitment to the new chain inside tags on the old chain, and resends the last key of the old chain for a while so receivers that missed it can catch up. Parameters T_0, T_int, d and N MUST NOT change during a session.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender locks each message with a key and promises to hand out the key a little later. Because keys follow a hidden chain, nobody can fake a later key without the earlier one.

sections.title: Bootstrapping and Time Synchronization
sections.content:
Before a receiver can check anything, it needs the sender's setup data and a secure idea of the sender's clock. The setup can arrive out of band, for example through MIKEY, or in band through a digitally signed bootstrap information message defined here. In both cases the receiver also needs the sender's public key or certificate, which this RFC does not tell you how to distribute.

TESLA depends on time, so receivers estimate an upper bound D_t on how far their clock lags the sender's. In direct synchronization the receiver sends a request with its time t_r and the sender answers with a signed response holding t_r and its own time t_s, giving D_t = t_s - t_r + S_sr. This needs a back channel, so it fits NORM better than ALC.

In indirect synchronization, sender and receivers each sync to an external reference such as authenticated NTP or SNTP, a GPS or Galileo device, or a clock with negligible drift. With one reference, D_t = D^O_t + D^R_t.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone needs to agree roughly what time it is, or a student could not tell whether a key was shown too early. They can ask the teacher directly, or all look at the same trusted clock.

sections.title: TESLA Messages in the EXT_AUTH Header Extension
sections.content:
TESLA information travels in the EXT_AUTH header extension of ALC and NORM packets. Each packet from the sender MUST carry exactly one. A 4-bit ASID field names the authentication scheme, and a 4-bit Type field says what the content is. Receivers that do not support TESLA MUST ignore the extension.

The bootstrap message is signed and carries the version, flags for single-chain, Group MAC and optional timing fields, the delay d, the algorithm types, T_int, T_0, the chain length N, the current interval index and the current key chain commitment. Because it is large, it MUST go in a stand-alone control packet.

Data packets use an authentication tag with the interval index i, a truncated MAC, and either the disclosed key K_{i-d}, no key, a commitment to a new chain, or the last key of the old chain. The tag without disclosure MUST be used during the first d intervals. The default function is HMAC-SHA-256, with keys of 256 bits and MACs truncated to 128 bits.

An optional Group MAC, made with a key shared by the whole group and typically truncated to 32 bits, lets receivers drop forged packets from outsiders at once. It does not help against a group member.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet gets a small label stuck on it. Most labels hold a seal and sometimes a revealed key, and one bigger label at the start explains the rules of the game.

sections.title: How a Receiver Verifies Packets
sections.content:
A receiver first discards everything except bootstrap and time-sync messages until TESLA is initialized. After that, each data packet goes through a series of checks. The first is the safe packet test: using D_t and the packet's arrival time, the receiver computes the highest interval the sender could be in, and if highest_i < i + d the key is not yet public, so the packet is safe to keep. Otherwise it MUST be discarded.

If a Group MAC is in use it is checked next, and a packet without one MUST be dropped. When the packet discloses a key, the receiver checks that key by running the one-way function until it reaches a key it already trusts. Packets that pass are buffered. Once the key for their interval is known, the receiver recomputes the MAC and keeps the packet only if it matches.

Receivers can skip needless work: packets for objects already decoded or unwanted may be discarded early, except ALC packets with the Close Session or Close Object flags. A sender that goes silent should keep sending empty packets with a standard tag for at least d intervals so the last keys are disclosed.
sections.plainLanguage: The student keeps each handout in a pile and only checks its seal after the teacher reveals the stamp. A handout that arrives after the stamp was already shown is thrown out, since it could be a fake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general TESLA concerns in RFC 4082 apply. Timing is critical, so D_t must be set correctly, and if the key disclosure schedule turns out to be wrong, the session MUST be closed and a new one started.

TESLA opens denial-of-service options. Forged packets cost the receiver computing and memory, since packets wait for key disclosure, and congestion control runs before authentication. The Group MAC is RECOMMENDED as a mitigation, and receivers should limit the memory spent on unauthenticated packets.

The RFC argues TESLA is robust to replays. Replayed bootstrap messages are ignored once a receiver is set up, replayed time-sync responses fail the checks, and a key chain that differs per session defeats replay across sessions. Any back channel used must have its own protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Troublemakers can flood the room with fake handouts to tire the students out, so the class can agree on a secret handshake to spot outsiders quickly.

messages.label: Time sync request
messages.note: Carries the receiver's local time t_r.

messages.label: Signed time sync response
messages.note: Carries t_r and the sender's time t_s; receiver computes D_t.

items.label: Bootstrap information
items.desc: Signed setup data, sent periodically or after a time sync request.

items.label: Standard Authentication Tag
items.desc: MAC plus the disclosed key for the ongoing chain.

items.label: Tag without Key Disclosure
items.desc: MAC only, for busy intervals and the first d intervals.

items.label: Tag with New Key Chain Commitment
items.desc: Sent near the end of a key chain.

items.label: Tag with Last Key of Old Chain
items.desc: Sent some time after moving to a new chain.

items.label: Direct time sync request
items.desc: Sent by a NORM receiver; invalid in ALC.

items.label: Direct time sync response
items.desc: Sent by a NORM sender; invalid in ALC.
